line: Phlebotomy, at St. Luke's. I take blood from forty people before breakfast. Very good for conversation. Nobody argues with the woman holding the needle.
Twenty-two years. My daughter Anjali says it's gross. She's sixteen and on the debate team, so she argues with me for practice. Today's topic was curfew.
I won. I'm the judge. Here, take this, it's avial from last night. Too much for three people. Bring the box back, the box is the important part.
choice1: Thank you. I'll bring the box back.

line: The radiator in 3C makes a sound like a pressure cooker. The super says it's normal. It's not normal. I know what a pressure cooker sounds like.
My walk. Doctor's orders, not mine. Anjali made me a playlist called 'Amma walking music.' It's all her debate warm-up songs.
choice1: Can I walk with you a bit?

line: Anjali has a tournament Saturday at the high school. Suresh has a shift. Will you come with me? I don't understand the scoring and I clap at the wrong time.
Good, we'll be confused together. Last time a judge asked her where she's from. She said 'here.' He said 'No, originally.' She said 'St. Luke's, third floor.'
choice3: I should go, but I'll be there.

line: I laughed in front of the judge. Anjali was mortified. Saturday, nine o'clock. Bring snacks. Debate parents are very competitive about snacks.
At work they asked us to report any patient who shows a foreign ID. We draw blood. We don't check passports. Three of us went to the manager together.
The hospital is paying for language classes for staff. I signed up for Spanish. Forty patients a morning, and half of them say 'ay' when the needle goes in.
choice2: You'll be fluent in a month.

line: You're at the hall every evening now. Mr. Deshpande will put you on the roof committee. He did it to Suresh. Suresh now has a spreadsheet.
You don't come to the hall anymore. Meena says you're at the library all the time. I'm only saying, the chai is better here.
